en: The Buddha’s Discourse on the Verses of the Dharma (*Buddhabhāṣita-dharmapada-sūtra*), Chapter One: The Preface on the Awakening of the Melted Hearts of All Bodhisattvas.
Thus have I heard. At one time, the Bhagavat was dwelling in the Palace of the Sun and Moon, upon the terrace of the Hall of Supreme Treasures.
He was accompanied by one hundred thousand Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas,
among whom were the Bodhisattva Jayagarbha and the Bodhisattva Samantabhadra.
Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva, Vajragarbha Bodhisattva,
and Vajradhvaja Bodhisattva.
Bodhisattva Vajramati,
Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara,
and Bodhisattva Niścayamati.
Maitreya Bodhisattva,
Triyadhvavikurvaṇa Bodhisattva,
and Nityapraṇidhāna Bodhisattva.
The Bodhisattva Sovereign Power,
the Bodhisattva Non-Arising Action,
and the Bodhisattva Constant Compassion.
The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Constantly Beholding the Radiance of the Single Mark was present,
along with a retinue of one hundred thousand such Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas.
Furthermore, there were other Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas.
His name was Ratnaprabhāsa.
Together with immeasurable bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs, he...
There were hundreds of thousands of laymen and laywomen.
Furthermore, there were immeasurable devas, nāgas, yakṣas,
and virtuous deities who protect the Dharma,
as well as countless bodhisattvas from other directions.
All had assembled. Chapter Two:
The Bodhisattva Abhedya-dharma Speaks of Past Causes and Conditions. Now, at that time...
In the assembly was a bodhisattva named Indestructible Jewel-Light of All Dharmas.
Empowered by the Buddha’s spiritual authority, he...
He then addressed the Buddha, saying,
"World-Honored One,
in the past, I left the household life to study the Way under the Buddha Dīpaṃkara."
At that time, the bhikṣu named Bhadrajyotis,
the World-Honored One then conferred upon me the prediction of my future attainment as a bodhisattva.
He was named "He Who Does Not Destroy Any Dharmas.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Ratnaprabha addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One,"
Why has the World-Honored One bestowed upon me the name "Jewel Radiance"?
I only pray that the World-Honored One will explain the reason for this name, Jewel Radiance.
The Buddha said:
"Listen attentively, listen attentively;
reflect upon this well."
Now, for the sake of those among the celestial hosts who seek the celestial vehicle,
I shall expound this definitive, subtle, and essential Dharma of the Mahāyāna,
as well as your name and the vajra phrases.
At that time, the assembly of devas received the instruction as they had heard it.
The Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva Ratnaprabhāsa:
"Good son," he said.
You should first observe these names of the Buddhas:
do they exist, or do they not exist?
"Is it real? Or is it unreal?
Good son."
If names were truly existent,
then even if one gave food to others by means of them,
one would never become satiated.
If one has attained non-existence,
which satiates all food and drink,
then there is nothing further to be used.
Why is this? Because it is said that one is immediately satiated upon hearing the name and has no further need for food.
If names did not exist...
Dīpaṃkara Tathāgata did not bestow upon me a prediction of enlightenment nor a name for you.
Since there was no one to grant such a prediction,
I would not have attained Buddhahood.
Good son, you should know that as for these syllables and phrases,
it is because they have existed for a long time and because they are such as they are.
The names and natures of all dharmas cultivated in meditation are empty;
they do not abide in existence or non-existence,
O son of good family.
If names are empty,
one should neither feel anger nor joy toward disparagement, slander,
censure, or praise. Why is this?
Because both slander and praise are equally empty. Chapter Three:
Contemplating the Emptiness of the Nature of Sound and Realizing the Limit of Reality. Good son, [listen].
If one encounters such circumstances as described above,
one should form this thought:
"Is this sound that of a deva or of a minor spirit?"
Blue, yellow, red, and white—
from which direction have you come?
Why have you now come to revile me?
"Where is this 'self' attached?
What is its form and appearance?
Observe it closely from top to bottom."
There is nothing at all to be obtained.
If there is nothing to be obtained,
one should not give rise to thoughts of anger or joy.
Having performed this contemplation,
one should firmly maintain it without abandoning it;
this should be known.
Before long, one shall attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Why is this? Because one contemplates that the nature of sound is empty.
Because they realize suchness.
For example, it is like a person who, while dreaming at night of flying through the air, sees their own body flying during sleep.
The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva is also just like this.
By contemplating that the nature of sound is empty, one will necessarily attain the realization of emptiness;
thus one knows that sounds merely deceive the auditory faculty and possess no substantial reality.
Chapter Four: Attaining Bodhi by Contemplating the Emptiness of the Three Bases.
Good son, the bodhisattva-mahāsattva...
Those who wish to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* should contemplate three locations: the internal,
the external, and the intermediate.
These are the three bases.
Within these three bases,
there is no real dharma.
This is itself liberation.
Liberation is itself bodhi.
The Bodhisattva Ratnaprabhā addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
what is meant by ‘observing the three bases’?
The Buddha told Baoming:
Good son, if you wish to know the three places,
you should cultivate the contemplation of the body.
The eye is internal;
visible forms are external;
the mind abides in between.
These are the three locations.
There are some sentient beings who,
from time immemorial, have [been thus].
Not knowing that these three matters are either empty or real,
they falsely give rise to various afflictions and fall into calamity;
therefore, I now teach you to contemplate them according to reality.
This causes all doubts to be severed. Good son,
the eye does not see itself.
Form does not name itself;
the mind has no physical substance.
These three things are all non-existent.
Therefore, the eye does not see itself;
it constantly abides within.
Form does not name itself.
It constantly abides externally;
the mind has no form or appearance,
and it dwells in no particular place.
Good son, the eye does not see itself;
it depends upon various causes and conditions.
The conditions do not possess the characteristic of being seen;
the eye itself is empty.
When form belongs to the eye, [it is likewise empty].
Name-and-form constitute form.
If the nature of the eye is empty,
then form also lacks reality.
Why is this? Because the body seen by the eye of emptiness has no substantial reality. Good son!
The bodhisattva mahāsattva knows that the eye is empty and is undefiled internally;
he knows that forms are empty and are unattached externally.
The consciousness-mind is empty and extinguishes all formations (*saṃskāra*).
It is the same for the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind. Good son!
Knowing that the eye belongs to conditions and lacks intrinsic nature,
though the eye sees all day long,
it is still without seeing.
The nature of form belongs to the eye and does not name itself;
though named all day long, it remains ultimately nameless. Good son!
With this eye of emptiness, one constantly contemplates empty forms;
observing both internally and externally, the mind cannot be apprehended.
One constantly seeks all forms, yet they can never be fully grasped.
The same applies to the ear and sounds, the nose and odors, the tongue and flavors, the body and tangibles,
and the mind and mental phenomena. Good son, you should form this thought:
If the eye and forms were not empty,
the eye abiding internally would not be distinguished from the external,
and forms abiding externally would not be perceived by the eye.
The eye has abiding;
forms also have abiding;
the mind is unconditioned.
It should not exist.
Why? Because existence and non-existence are mutually contradictory in their essential natures.
Therefore, you should know that the eye,
forms, and the mind are empty, pervasive,
and unimpeded. Good son!
The mind is internal;
dharmas are external; the mental faculty (manas) is situated between them.
The mind does not know itself;
phenomena do not name themselves;
the mind has no form or characteristics.
Since these three factors are all absent,
the mind does not know itself;
it constantly abides within.
The Dharma does not name itself;
it eternally abides beyond.
The mind has no form or characteristics.
In reality, there is no location;
the mind does not know itself,
being dependent upon various causes and conditions.
Conditions do not possess the characteristic of cognition;
the mind itself is emptiness.
When phenomena belong to the mind, those phenomena are designated as "phenomena."
If the nature of the mind is empty, then phenomena are likewise without reality. Why?
Because from an empty mind, one knows that the essence is devoid of intrinsic nature.
Good son, know that the mind is empty;
thus, there is no defilement within.
Knowing that phenomena are empty,
one is without attachment to external things;
knowing that the mind is empty.
He brings all conditioned formations to cessation;
he knows that the mind is dependent upon conditions and that it lacks intrinsic nature.
The mind may know throughout the entire day, yet it remains without knowing;
the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) belongs to the mind, yet it does not name itself.
A name may be applied throughout the entire day, yet it remains without a name.
With this mind of emptiness, one should constantly know the dharmas of emptiness.
Observing both internally and externally, the mind is found to be ungraspable.
Therefore, a bodhisattva should form this thought:
If the mind and mental objects were not empty,
the mind would abide internally and could not discern external objects;
mental objects would abide externally and could not arise from the mind.
The mental faculty (manas) is a conditioned phenomenon that abides;
the mind (citta), being unconditioned (asaṃskṛta), should not abide within [the conditioned]. Why is this?
Because existence and non-existence are mutually exclusive by nature,
one should therefore know that the mental objects (dharma) and the mind are as unimpeded as space.
For example, a mirage appears like water when viewed from afar;
a person lacking wisdom, driven by the urge to obtain it, rushes toward it,
yet as he draws closer, it vanishes.
Those dwelling at the edge of the flames know that there has been no water in this place from the very beginning;
seeing those people running away, they recognize their false perceptions and break into laughter, saying to the runners:
In this place there is no water, but only hot vapors;
they deceive your visual faculty.
Upon hearing this, that person’s feverish thirst subsides.
Form is also like this.
Ordinary people, lacking wisdom, claim it has substantial reality;
driven by the thirst of desire, they give rise to the signs of craving and seeking.
With a burning mind, one rushes toward and pursues them;
yet as they depend on conditions, their forms shift and their perceptions cease.
One who realizes the true nature knows that within these aggregates, form has been non-existent from the very beginning.
Originally there is no consciousness;
seeing that ordinary people greedily pursue forms,
one quickly realizes it is but a deluded thought.
They then broke into derisive laughter.
He spoke the true Dharma for them,
and the people said:
Within the aggregates there are no aggregates;
within the mind there is no mind;
within thought there is no thought.
It is merely conditioned by the vital breath,
deceiving your visual faculty.
If there were one who possessed wisdom, [they would not be so deluded].
Having heard this, the false thirst of the mind subsides;
the aggregates, elements, and sense bases are likewise so,
O son of good family.
For example, it is like an ordinary person who, in a night dream,
sees their own body emitting various kinds of light and eating food of a hundred flavors.
Furthermore, he sees himself traveling far away to another land,
where he obtains fine clothing and horses.
Although his attendants employed every means [to pacify him],
he suddenly gave rise to anger and immediately commanded his forces.
He killed several thousand people.
When he awoke, the radiance of his body immediately vanished.
Nor does it travel far;
the appearance of its luminous color is empty and non-existent.
The practitioner in the dream,
as well as the appearance of the ritual force,
and the one who kills— none of these possess any material form or characteristics.
Form is also like this.
All sentient beings,
from beginningless time until now, [have been thus].
Beneath the precipice of darkness,
one is submerged in ignorance,
slumbering through the long night.
Abiding within the dream-house,
one falsely perceives various forms and gives rise to all phenomena.
Virtuous sons and virtuous daughters,
saṃsāra and nirvāṇa slay and harm one another.
It is inexhaustible.
All sentient beings claim that they have truly attained the Way;
only the Awakened One knows it to be illusory, and thus first realizes that birth and death share the same characteristic as nirvana.
The various forms of men and women are by their very nature and essence empty. Good son!
If form is thus,
so too are all phenomena; they are like an echo in an empty valley.
It is as unsubstantial as a plantain tree;
it is like the moon reflected in water;
it is like a flower in the sky.
Like the son of a barren woman;
like lightning remaining for a long time;
like the hair of a tortoise in water.
Just as the horns of a running rabbit are ultimately non-existent,
those who possess wisdom should eliminate all views.
It is like one born blind in this world who cannot differentiate forms;
if one does not differentiate them, [one remains so].
You should know, O sons and daughters of good family, that all sentient beings will before long attain the path of Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Because they are obscured by various afflictions, those who lack the cause for wisdom perceive the eye where there is no eye;
through such forgetful conceptualization, they perceive external objects,
which are termed "form" (rūpa).
Just as one gives rise to craving and attachment,
by virtue of that craving and attachment,
one wanders through the three realms of existence.
It is like a whirling firebrand that never ceases.
Chapter Five: Approaching True Spiritual Friends. "Good son, [approaching true spiritual friends...]"
All sentient beings who wish to attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi should draw near to spiritual friends.
"I request the essential points of the Dharma;
I must surely hear such profound and essential phrases.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Ratnaprabhā addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
what is a spiritual friend?
The Buddha said:
A virtuous friend is one who skillfully understands the profound Dharma of emptiness, signlessness, wishlessness, non-arising, and non-ceasing;
they thoroughly comprehend that all phenomena have been ultimately equal from the very beginning.
Without karma, without retribution, without cause, and without effect, its nature and characteristics are suchness (tathatā).
Abiding in the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi),
it is vigorously established within ultimate emptiness (atyanta-śūnyatā).
This is called a spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*).
Chapter Six: Twenty-one Similes on the Spiritual Friend. Good son, [the following are the twenty-one similes for the spiritual friend].
A spiritual friend is your parent,
for they nurture your bodhi-body;
a spiritual friend is the cause of your eyes.
Because they show and guide you along the path to enlightenment,
spiritual friends are your feet; for they carry you across,
leading you away from birth and death.
A spiritual friend is your ladder,
for they support you until you reach the other shore.
A spiritual friend is your food and drink.
Because they enable you to increase the Dharma-body,
virtuous friends are your precious refuge;
because they cover you so that you may attain the body of merit.
A spiritual friend is your bridge,
for they transport you across the ocean of existence.
A spiritual friend is your wealth and treasure.
I rescue and sustain you because of your poverty and suffering.
A spiritual friend is your sun and moon,
for they illuminate you so that you may leave behind the darkness.
A spiritual friend is your very life,
for there is no time when they do not protect and cherish you;
a spiritual friend is your armor and weaponry.
Because they subdue all māras and attain fearlessness;
because spiritual friends are your ropes and pulleys for pulling you out of hell;
and because spiritual friends are your sublime medicine.
Because they treat the disease of your afflictions,
spiritual friends are like sharp knives for you,
severing the net of all your attachments.
A spiritual friend is your timely rain,
for he moistens and purifies your bodhi-bodies.
A spiritual friend is your bright lamp.
Because they are able to shatter the darkness of your five hindrances,
spiritual friends are your excellent signposts;
for they instruct you in how to proceed upon the right path.
A spiritual friend is your fuel and fire,
for he brings to maturity the food of nirvana for you all.
A spiritual friend is your bow and arrow.
Because they shoot and slay the thieves of your afflictions;
spiritual friends are your heroic acquisitions,
for they are able to shatter the army of your birth and death.
A spiritual friend is your Tathāgata,
for he destroys your afflictions and leads you to nirvāṇa. Good son!
A spiritual friend possesses such immeasurable merit.
For this reason, I now instruct you to draw near to them.
Chapter Seven: The Assembly of Precious Radiance Overwhelmed by Compassion. At that time, the assembly of Precious Radiance...
Together with the assembly of devas,
having heard the Buddha preach this sublime Dharma and the profound, essential Dharma of the spiritual friends,
they raised their voices and wailed.
Tears fell like rain;
he wailed with grief and distress,
unable to compose himself.
He thought to himself:
"From time immemorial,
my own body has been protected by spiritual friends."
Therefore, having encountered the Tathāgata today,
one is able to hear the profound Dharma.
To meet [him] in such a way—
This is the power of spiritual friends;
it is not by our own power that we can reflect upon this.
We have never before repaid their kindness, yet now we draw near to them.
Having spoken these words,
he raised his voice once more to wail in grief and distress;
beating his breast, he wept like a god.
It is, for example, like a person who has recently lost their parents and is wailing and weeping in grief.
Having died, he was restored to life.
At that time, the World-Honored One,
having witnessed this event, [spoke].
Giving rise to a heart of compassion,
he immediately let out a long sigh; by virtue of this sighing,
the trichiliocosm was shaken and vibrated.
All Buddha-fields likewise shook greatly.

Chapter Eight: The Chapter on the Testimony of Faith by the Bodhisattva Samantaprabhālaṃkāra and Others. Now, in the eastern direction, there was a land within hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of asaṃkhyeya worlds.
The land is named Ratnabhūmi.
The Buddha is named Ratnalakṣaṇa.
There is a bodhisattva there.
It was named Universal Radiance Adornment.
Seeing this earth tremble, he addressed the Buddha White Jewel Mark, saying,
"World-Honored One!"
"What is the auspicious omen of this earthquake?
That Buddha replied, "To the west,
beyond hundreds of thousands of myriads of koṭis of asaṃkhyeya lands, there is a country."
It is named Sahā;
the Buddha’s title is Śākyamuni,
who expounds the Buddha-dharma for the sake of all sentient beings.
To demonstrate his resolve in the Mahāyāna and to repay the kindness of his spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra),
he manifested this auspicious omen.
The Bodhisattva Samantaprabhālaṃkāra addressed the Buddha Ratnākṣa, saying:
"Bhagavān,
I wish to go together with this assembly of devas to that Sahā world."
Śākyamuni Buddha requested this teaching;
he served spiritual friends and inquired about the profound Dharma.
The Buddha Ratnaketu said,
"Good son, this is the very time;
you should dwell [in this state] with swift diligence."
Thereupon, the Bodhisattva Samantaprabhālaṃkāra,
together with immeasurable deva-bodhisattvas,
each manifested their own bodies.
Seated upon a lion throne of precious lotuses,
emitting celestial radiance like that of a divine *mahābala*,
he bent his body and extended his arm to reach as far as the Sahā world.
It remained serenely in the midst of space.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Ratnaprabhāsa, beholding this manifestation of light,
addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Blessed One,
what is this radiance?
It is the first time I have ever seen such a thing."
The Buddha addressed the great assembly and the Bodhisattva Ratnaprabhāsa, saying:

"This is the sign of the earth’s trembling that the devas and bodhisattvas of the Tathāgata Ratnalakṣaṇa have heard me preach for you this Mahāyāna sūtra and the manifestation of the spiritual friend."
Therefore, when the Bodhisattva Ratnaprabhāsa and the great assembly arrived and heard these words,
they were all filled with great joy.
[He adjusted] his robes and stood to the left and right of the Buddha. Thereupon,
the Bodhisattva Samantaprabhālaṃkāra...
From the midst of the void,
a rain of various precious flowers fell;
having finished raining down these flowers, [the assembly remained].
He soon arrived at the place where Śākyamuni Buddha was,
circumambulated him countless times, joined his palms in prostration, and stood to one side.
The Buddha then addressed the Bodhisattva Universal Radiance Adornment, saying:
"Noble son,
when you set out, was your World-Honored One’s strength and vigor well?
Having traveled such a long distance, I hope you have not been fatigued?"
The Bodhisattva Samantaprabhālaṃkṛta prostrated at the Buddha’s feet and replied,
“At that time, O World-Honored One,
my physical strength and vitality were always such as they are now; there was no other.”
Having offered these earnest instructions and extended boundless greetings,
Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva, amidst the assembly,
addressed the Bodhisattva Samantaprabhālaṃkāra, saying:
"O sons of good family, you have come from afar; what do you wish to inquire about?
Thus spoke the Bodhisattva Samantaprabhālaṃkṛta.
He addressed Mañjuśrī, saying,
"Virtuous One,
I have received from the World-Honored One the teaching of the profound Dharma."
And regarding all the merits of a spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra).
For this reason, I have come wishing to inquire about certain matters concerning the merits possessed by a spiritual friend.
Mañjuśrī said, "If there are those who wish to inquire,
they should quickly put their questions forth."
"This great assembly wishes to hear this with joy. Thereupon,
the Bodhisattva Universal Radiance Adornment, knowing the intention of the assembly,
stepped forward, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
World-Honored One,
until now our power of wisdom has been weak;
we have not been able to skillfully resolve or determine the profound and subtle meaning of the Mahāyāna.
Furthermore, it is as previously stated by the Buddha: that spiritual friends (kalyāṇamitra) possess no [ordinary] debt of gratitude;
rather, their kindness is so profound as to be difficult to calculate.
"I only pray that the World-Honored One will, for the sake of this great assembly,
expound the Dharma on how to draw near to spiritual friends.
The Buddha said:
Excellent, excellent!
Son of good family,
you are truly able to inquire about such a Dharma for the sake of all sentient beings.
Listen attentively, listen attentively;
reflect upon it well.
I shall speak for you.
Chapter Nine: Afflictions are Enlightenment. Good son, spiritual friends possess great merit;
they are able to establish you within the Buddha-dharma amidst desire, hatred, ignorance, and false views, as well as among the five hindrances, the five desires, and the various defilements.
By not giving rise to a single thought, one attains great merit.
It is like a person who, aboard a sturdy ship, crosses the great ocean;
with body and mind unmoving, they reach the further shore.
A spiritual friend is also like this:
with the ship of great vows, they dwell within the ocean of birth and death to transport you all across.
Without moving body or mind,
one reaches the shore of nirvana. Good son!
It is, for example, as if there were a person wishing to travel a perilous road who relies upon another individual skilled in the arts, well-equipped with armor and weapons,
possessing a fine chariot drawn by five horses.
Body and mind are free from fear,
and one attains mastery without difficulty;
a spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra) is likewise so.
The Dharmakāya is robust and skilled in expedient means;
it possesses the arts of the six perfections and the armor and weapons of compassion and loving-kindness.
They have all cultivated existence and,
having come to the Great Vehicle, they employ the five supernormal powers to transport you all so that you may attain fearlessness.
They shall be freed from the various hardships of birth and death within the three miserable realms. Good son,
it is like a person who, by relying on the Laṅkā jewel and taking the wondrous medicine of ambrosia, eliminates all illnesses.
One’s life shall not be cut short prematurely.

A virtuous friend is likewise so: by relying on the jewel of great wisdom and taking the medicine of the Dharma, one eliminates the disease of afflictions, and the life of wisdom becomes inexhaustible.
Good son, it is like a person who,
by relying on the lion king, moves among all the beasts without any fear.
A virtuous friend is also like this:
if there is one who relies upon them,
even while wandering amidst the afflictions of worldly toil, they shall have nothing to fear.
Good son, it is like a person who relies upon Mount Sumeru;
even if the eight winds were to blow, they could not move him.
Relying upon a spiritual friend is likewise so:
the winds of the eight difficulties cannot blow them away. Good son!
It is like a person who, relying on the garuḍa, surveys the great ocean from all sides;
they do not fear any calamities,
nor the perils posed by the makara fish.
Relying upon a spiritual friend is likewise so:
one traverses the ocean of birth and death without fearing the perils of demons or non-Buddhists. Good son!
As for a spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra),
their immeasurable merits are vast;
should one wish to describe them in detail:
Exhausting kalpas without end. Chapter Ten:
Seeking a Spiritual Friend Without Borrowing from Internal or External Life-Span; A Chapter on Suspicions. If there is one who possesses wisdom:
Upon seeing a spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*), one should make offerings even at the cost of body and life;
how much more so should one not be stingy with wealth, kinsmen, wife, children, or kingdoms and cities?
Regarding whatever actions or various circumstances a spiritual friend may encounter, one should not give rise to even a hair’s breadth of doubt.
Why is this? If one harbors doubt, one will not attain right reception (*samyaksamādhi*) regarding the profound phrases of the Dharma.
"You, the great assembly, should sever all doubts regarding the spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*).
Chapter Eleven: The Universal Radiance Questions the Tathāgata on Compassion and the Response in Verse. At that time, the Bodhisattva Universal Radiance Adornment addressed the Buddha, saying:
World-Honored One,
how does one correctly receive these profound phrases of the Dharma?
What is meant by "profound"?
The Buddha said,
"Do not ask such a question.
If it were spoken now, the śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and bodhisattvas who have newly resolved their minds would find their hearts oppressed upon hearing this teaching."
[They] sever and destroy the roots of goodness.
The Bodhisattva Samantaprabhālaṃkara addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One,"
"Please teach us through skillful means so that we may perform future deeds for the sake of all sentient beings.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
Sons of the Buddha, listen well and attentively; I shall now speak according to reality.
The nature of all phenomena is fundamentally unmoving. It is by relying on greed and hatred that the Buddhas sit within the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*);
the seeds of the Buddhas are found within afflictions, fundamentally unmoving—so too are the five hindrances and the five desires.
As the lineage of the Tathāgatas, they are always adorned by this; From the beginning, they have been unmoving.
Lust, perverse views, And all other fetters and afflictions— The characteristic of ultimate liberation is that from the beginning they have been unmoving.
All Buddhas, from the very beginning, Constantly abide within the three poisons.
Nurturing the hundred dharmas, just as one accomplishes the state of a World-Honored One;
all dharmas from the very beginning are neither existent nor non-existent, for the nature of existence and non-existence is quiescent. From the beginning, there has been no movement;
for all sentient beings, in reality, there is neither arising nor ceasing—arising and ceasing are themselves nirvāṇa.
Fundamentally unmoving are the characteristics of all phenomena; Arising from conditions, they have no creator, and the nature of creation is suchness.
Fundamentally unmoving, all written words are without reality and without basis;
They are all equally one in quiescent extinction, fundamentally unmoving.
Regarding all merits of giving, the three factors therein are empty; ultimately, the merit of giving cannot be apprehended, being like a mirage.
If one speaks of the various forms of upholding the precepts—wherein there is neither "good" nor "proper conduct"—the nature of the precepts is like space;
those who uphold them are deluded. If one sees one who is full of anger...
Taking patience as one’s harness and bridle, knowing that anger and the like are like a mirage, and that even patience has nothing to be patient with—this is what is called the practice of diligence.
To speak of it for those with overweening pride is to speak for the sake of increasing their arrogance;
for one who is free from overweening pride, there is neither "good" nor "diligence. If one gives rise to a mind of striving, this is delusion and not true diligence.
If one can keep the mind from wandering and practice with diligent sincerity, then even if one studies various samādhis, these are merely movements and not true seated meditation.
When the mind flows along with external objects, how can it be called concentration?
The myriad phenomena are encompassed by a single seal; how is it that within this single dharma, [all things are found]?
Just as various views arise, even the "one" is not truly one.
This is intended to shatter all numerical categories heard by those of shallow wisdom; they perceive the one and take it to be one.
If there are those who hear this Dharma and constantly cultivate the practice of quiescence, knowing that cognition itself is also quiescent—this is the path to Bodhi.
If one wishes to realize this Dharma, one should draw near to virtuous friends (*kalyāṇamitra*) and skillfully train in all means (*upāya*) to liberate all beings.
I now teach this Dharma in order to gather those sentient beings who are free from the view of self (*ātman*).
For those who have reached the ultimate end where there is nothing to be said, these are the vajra-words.
Having decisively resolved all false views, None among the ranks of all externalists Can ever destroy it, even with all their might.
If there are sentient beings Who manage to hear such a sutra as this, Though they remain within the three miserable realms, They will ultimately attain the bliss of cool serenity.
If one hears the name of this sutra, Or understands the meaning of even a single phrase, [they shall likewise attain liberation].
They will surely be born in the lands of all Buddhas, How much more so for those who read and recite it! Wherever this sutra may be, I shall always be present therein;
To protect such persons as these, I cause them to attain the Unsurpassed Way. 12. Chapter on Bestowing Prophecy.

At that time, after the World-Honored One had spoken these verses, the great assembly of Universal Radiance attained the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*). This is the twelfth chapter, "Bestowing Prophecy to Ratnaprabha. Immediately thereafter, the Bodhisattva Ratnaprabha received his prophecy.
In a future age, after eighty thousand kalpas have passed, you shall attain Buddhahood.
You shall be known as Ratnaprabhāsa Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidhyācaraṇasaṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavān.
At that time, there will be sentient beings who are exclusively of the Mahāyāna,
with no śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas at all.
The name of that land is Adorned and Pure;
it surpasses that of Amitāyus by hundreds of thousands of millions of times.
Having finished bestowing predictions of enlightenment upon all the bodhisattvas, [the Buddha said:]
He then wished to leave his seat.
Chapter Thirteen: On the Transmission and Maintenance. At that time, the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī came forward and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Blessed One,
in the hands of what kind of people will these [teachings] be in the future?
By what karmic conditions and through what grace shall they hear this sutra?"
The Buddha said, "Good son,
this sutra is extremely profound and difficult to hear."
For example, just as no ordinary person can behold a vajra,
with the sole exception of Śakra,
so too is this sutra.
It cannot be seen by śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas;
it is only the Bodhisattvas who can behold it,
just as among all birds and beasts, none dare approach a lion.
With the sole exception of the dragon kings,
this sutra is likewise so:
it cuts off all expectations of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.
Except for bodhisattvas,
even if someone were to fill the four continents with pure gold and give it as a gift,
the merit gained from hearing the name of this sutra would be ten thousand times greater.
Suppose there were someone who, using nothing but the seven precious gems, fashioned couches and seats,
and offered garments of crystal to sentient beings,
filling the entire realm of Jambudvīpa.
The merit gained by hearing the name of this sutra for a single kalpa is ten thousand times greater than that.
If there are good sons or good daughters who are able to hear this sutra, [they shall obtain such merit].
You should know that this person has personally attended upon countless Buddhas and planted many roots of virtue.
Only then can one hear it.
Good son, this sutra shall,
in the future, come into the hands of Bodhisattvas of the eighth stage.
Chapter Fourteen: Guarding the Sūtra as One’s Eyes—Better to Lose Body and Life than Neglect It. The Buddha addressed the great assembly and the Bodhisattva Ratnaprabhāsa:
You must protect this sutra as you would your own eyes;
you would rather lose your body and life than let it be lost.
Do not give rise to indolence regarding this sutra.
If there are sentient beings...
Those who give rise to faith in this sutra should know that such persons are truly disciples of the Buddha; of this there is no doubt.
At that time, when the World-Honored One had finished preaching this sutra,
the entire great assembly— the eight classes of beings, including devas and nāgas— were all filled with joy and practiced accordingly in accordance with the Dharma.
